title: Agatha (5 February)
hookLine: a Sicilian martyr, named at Mass, patron of Catania and of breast cancer patients

lines: A ROLL CALL INSIDE THE MASS.
cards: At Mass, when the priest prays the Roman Canon, Eucharistic Prayer One, there's a moment near the end when he reads a little roll call of martyrs.
Among them is a run of women's names: Felicity, Perpetua, Agatha, Lucy, Agnes, Cecilia, Anastasia. It goes by fast.
But every time that prayer is said, a young woman from Sicily is named at the altar, alongside the apostles. The third name on that list: Agatha.

teach.b: Agatha was a martyr of Catania, in Sicily, in the age of Roman persecution. That the Church honored her is clear: her name is in the Canon itself.
The details come from a later account of her martyrdom, which the Church hands on as her story. In it, Agatha is a young Christian woman who has given her life to God.
A powerful Roman official wants her, and when she refuses him, he turns her faith into a charge against her. She's sent away to be broken down, and isn't.

teach.h: A REFUSAL, A TRIAL, A WOUND.
teach.b: At her trial she answers calmly. Then she's tortured, and the account is unflinching: her breasts are cut off.
That night in prison, the story says, the apostle Peter comes to her in a vision and heals her wounds. She dies soon after, still refusing. It's a hard story.

teach.h: PATRON OF WOMEN WITH BREAST CANCER.
teach.b: Tradition has made Agatha, who suffered in her body, a patron of women with breast cancer, and of nurses. Her city keeps her too.
In Catania, people carry her relics through the streets on her feast, and tradition says that when the volcano Etna threatened the city, her veil was carried out to meet the lava.
Paul, in his second letter to the Corinthians, hears Christ speak to him in his own weakness.

teach.h: MY GRACE IS SUFFICIENT FOR THEE.
teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims: "My grace is sufficient for thee". Some readers hear Agatha's story in that line: a body hurt beyond fairness, and a grace that held.

how: Catholics keep Saint Agatha's memorial in February; in Catania her feast is a great city festival with processions of her relics, and some hospitals and cancer support groups take her as patron.

o: a Sicilian martyr named in the Mass's Canon
a Roman empress who protected Christians
an abbess who nursed plague victims

p: where her name is read at Mass
heals her in prison, in her story

s: Agatha's name is read in one of the Eucharistic Prayers of the Mass
in the Roman Canon, between Perpetua and Lucy.
Agatha was a nun in a Sicilian convent
her story makes her a young woman who had given her life to God, living in her own city.
Agatha agreed to the official's demands to save her life
she refused, and was tortured and died a martyr.

games.q: you're Agatha. a powerful official wants you, and he can turn your faith into a crime. what do you do?
o: give in, and keep your faith in secret.
games.why: in her story she refused, answered calmly at trial, was tortured, and died a martyr.

practice: Bring to mind someone who has cancer now, or has had it, or someone who cares for them, and hold their name gently, the way a friend sits by a bed, without trying to fix anything.
If you pray, ask Saint Agatha to pray for them; if you don't, wish them strength and good care, and let the name rest.

wordCard.voice: Agatha. A martyr of Catania in Sicily, named in the Roman Canon at Mass, and honored as a patron of women with breast cancer.

orig.note: Greek: Agatha's name; agathos is the Greek word for good.

carryVoice: Your line: agatha of sicily. Her name is still said at the altar. Until tomorrow.
